newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish court upholds law boosting taxman's powers.
newsitem.headline: Polish court upholds law boosting taxman's powers.

text.p: Poland's Constitutional Tribunal on Tuesday upheld a law allowing tax inspectors easier access to bank accounts, overruling objections by the country's ombudsman that it infringed citizen's rights to privacy.

PAP news agency said the tribunal ruled that the recent law, obliging banks and financial institutions to divulge information about clients' accounts on request by tax offices, or face fines, was in keeping with the constitution.
The new law removed a previous requirement that tax offices had to get special permission to check bank accounts from courts, prosecutors or the heads of one of two major state inspection offices.
The ombudsman's office objected that this constituted access to citizens' private lives which was "unlimited, uncontrolled and not subject to appeal," PAP said.

It argued that the law infringed a constitutional right to privacy of correspondence and a clause saying that Poland was a democratic country ruled by law which honoured international human rights conventions.

A finance ministry representative at the hearing argued that the right to secrecy of correspondence could be infringed in justified cases and pointed to the example of Sweden, where he said banks were practically branches of the tax offices.

The tribunal agreed that the principle of confidentiality was not absolute and that less rigid banking secrecy could limit tax crimes, while tax office confidentiality regulations, enforced by law, safeguarded personal information.

But the court decided that a clause allowing the finance minister to make public tax arrears of people and firms doing business infringed privacy rights and that such a penalty should only be decided by a court, PAP said.
This decision means parliament must now either change this aspect of the law within six months or muster a two-thirds majority to overturn the tribunal's ruling.
